slides.title: Supply Chain
points: Supply-chain attacks compromise a trusted upstream provider, vendor, supplier, or service so attackers can reach downstream customers.
Security+ Objective 2.2: explain common threat vectors and attack surfaces.

slides.title: Supply Chain
slides.teach: The broader ecosystem of organizations, software, hardware, and services that contribute to a product or business operation.

course.learn: The broader ecosystem of organizations, software, hardware, and services that contribute to a product or business operation.

breakdown.explanation: The attacker compromises something trusted upstream to reach downstream victims.
Software dependencies, Hardware suppliers, Service providers

course.why: Organizations inherit risk from third parties they trust.
course.example: A trusted software update is modified before customers download it.
course.exam: Compromise upstream, reach customers → SUPPLY CHAIN.
course.check_q: What type of attack abuses a trusted upstream provider?

slides.title: Managed Service Providers (MSPs)
slides.teach: Third parties that remotely manage or support customer systems.

course.learn: Third parties that remotely manage or support customer systems.

breakdown.explanation: One provider may have privileged access to many customers.
IT management provider, Remote monitoring provider

course.why: Compromising one MSP can give attackers a path into multiple customer environments.
course.example: Attackers steal an MSP's remote-management credentials and use them against several clients.
course.check_q: Which supply-chain entity remotely manages many customer systems?

slides.title: Vendors
slides.teach: Organizations that sell or provide products or services used by another organization.

course.learn: Organizations that sell or provide products or services used by another organization.

breakdown.explanation: A trusted company provides something your organization uses.

course.why: A compromised vendor can distribute malicious updates, services, or credentials to customers.
course.example: A software vendor's update infrastructure is compromised.
course.check_q: Which entity provides a product or service used by the organization?

slides.title: Suppliers
slides.teach: Organizations that provide components, materials, hardware, software, or services within the supply chain.

course.learn: Organizations that provide components, materials, hardware, software, or services within the supply chain.

breakdown.explanation: They provide upstream components or resources.

course.why: Compromised components can enter downstream products before they reach customers.
course.example: Malicious hardware components enter the manufacturing chain.
course.check_q: Which entity provides upstream components in a supply chain?

blocks.title: Who in the trusted chain was compromised?
items: Compromise upstream, reach customers → SUPPLY CHAIN
The attacker abuses trust in a third party instead of attacking each victim directly.
Example: A trusted software update is modified before customers receive it.
MSPs often have privileged access into many customer environments.
Example: Attackers steal an MSP's remote-management credentials.
The organization relies on a vendor's product or service.
Example: A software vendor's update infrastructure is compromised.
The problem begins with an upstream component source.
Example: Malicious hardware components enter the manufacturing chain.
blocks.example: Memory: Supply chain = upstream trust · MSP = manages many · Vendor = provides product/service · Supplier = provides components.

questions.q: A trusted software update is modified before customers download it. Which attack type best fits?
questions.explanation: The attacker compromises a trusted upstream source to reach downstream customers.

questions.q: Attackers steal a remote-management provider's credentials and use them to access several customers. Which supply-chain entity was compromised?
questions.explanation: An MSP remotely manages customer systems and may have broad privileged access.

questions.q: A software company's update infrastructure is compromised and malicious code reaches customers. Which third party is most directly described?
questions.explanation: The company provides software used by customers, making it a vendor.

questions.q: Malicious components are introduced before hardware reaches the manufacturer. Which supply-chain entity is most relevant?
questions.explanation: Suppliers provide upstream components or materials.

questions.q: Why are MSPs attractive supply-chain targets?
choices: One compromise may provide access to many customer environments
They cannot be trusted by customers
questions.explanation: MSPs often manage multiple clients using privileged remote access.
